pos: n. (John Willock, d. 1585, superintendent of Glasgow and the west, one of the Scottish reformers)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Scots Willock, a diminutive of William, resolute protector.
biblical_def: John Willock was a Scottish friar who fled to England under Henry VIII, served as chaplain to the Duke of Suffolk, took refuge in Emden under Mary, and came home as a physician and a preacher at the point when Scotland was deciding. In 1559, when Knox was away and the Lords of the Congregation were at their lowest, Willock preached in St Giles' and held Edinburgh's pulpit through the crisis; it was he who was asked, in the council, whether the regent might lawfully be suspended from her authority, and his careful answer helped carry the point. He was named superintendent of Glasgow and the west in 1560, one of the five, and helped draw the First Book of Discipline. He spent his later years holding an English living in Leicestershire while returning to Scotland for the assemblies, which the Scots resented and endured. Willock is the man who stood in the gap when the famous one was absent, which happens in every reformation and is almost never remembered. “Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong” (1Co 16:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines superintendent as one who has the oversight and charge of something, and regent as one who governs a kingdom during the minority or absence of the king.
webster_full: SUPERINTEND'ENT, n. One who has the oversight and charge of something, with the power of direction.
RE'GENT, n. One invested with vicarious authority; one who governs a kingdom in the minority or disability of the king.
CONGREGA'TION, n. An assembly of persons; a collection of people met for the worship of God.
PHYSI'CIAN, n. A person skilled in the art of healing; one whose profession is to prescribe remedies for diseases.

Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
Pro 29:2
When the righteous are in authority, the people rejoice: but when the wicked beareth rule, the people mourn.
corruption_summary: The man who held St Giles' in 1559 while Knox was away.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the reduction of the Scottish Reformation to one man, with the result that the five superintendents and the rest of the ministry become supporting cast in a biography. Willock preached the Edinburgh pulpit at the hinge of the whole business and gave the council the judgment it needed on the regent's authority, and he is a footnote.

The principle to recover is Ezekiel's, where the Lord describes what he looks for and what he did not find. “And I sought for a man among them, that should make up the hedge, and stand in the gap before me for the land, that I should not destroy it: but I found none” (Eze 22:30). The gap is a place, not an office, and it is filled by whoever is there. Paul's charge to the Ephesian elders assumes the same: “Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock” (Act 20:28).

pos: n. (John Winram, c. 1492–1582, subprior of St Andrews and superintendent of Fife)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Scots Winram, from a Lothian place-name.
biblical_def: John Winram spent thirty years as subprior of the great priory of St Andrews and then became superintendent of Fife under the reformed church, which makes him the most awkward figure in the Scottish settlement. He had sat on the assize that condemned George Wishart to the fire in 1546 and preached the sermon before the burning, and he had examined Patrick Hamilton. He had also, through all those years, been quietly protecting men suspected of heresy within the priory and failing to prosecute when he could have. When the Reformation came in 1560 he conformed at once, helped draft the First Book of Discipline, and governed Fife as superintendent for twenty years with no recorded complaint against his doctrine. Scotland let him. The question his life puts is a hard one and ought not to be softened: how much weight does late and useful service carry against earlier compliance in a judicial murder? The reformed church answered by using him and not by exonerating him, which may be as near as men can get. “Whosoever therefore shall confess me before men, him will I confess also before my Father which is in heaven” (Mat 10:32).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines subprior as the vicegerent of a prior, and conform as to comply with, to bring into harmony with an established form.
webster_full: SUBPRI'OR, n. The vicegerent of a prior; a claustral officer who assists the prior.
CONFORM', v. To comply with or yield to; to live or act according to, as to a rule or precept.
AS'SIZE, n. A court of justice; a jury; the trial of a cause by a jury.
TEM'PORIZE, v. To comply with the time or occasion; to yield to prevailing opinion or circumstances.

corruption_summary: The subprior who preached before Wishart's burning and governed Fife for the reformed church.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the smoothing of a record like Winram's into a story of gradual enlightenment, as though a man who sat on the assize that burned George Wishart and later became a Protestant superintendent had simply travelled a road at his own pace. He did travel it. He also preached the sermon at that burning, and the reformed church that employed him never pretended otherwise.

The principle to recover is the one John records of men in exactly Winram's position, and it is stated without sympathy or scorn, as a fact: “among the chief rulers also many believed on him; but because of the Pharisees they did not confess him, lest they should be put out of the synagogue” (Joh 12:42). The Lord's own word on the matter is a pair of sentences that leave no third place to stand: “Whosoever therefore shall confess me before men, him will I confess also before my Father which is in heaven” (Mat 10:32), and the converse follows it.

pos: n. (John Row, c. 1526–1580, papal canon lawyer turned Scottish reformer, minister of Perth)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Scots Row, from a northern surname, dweller by the row of houses.
biblical_def: John Row was sent to Rome in 1550 as the agent of the Scottish clergy, took a doctorate in canon law, and was returning in 1558 as papal nuncio to deal with the spreading heresy in Scotland when he read himself out of his own commission. He examined the question he had been sent to suppress, concluded that the reformers were right, and joined them. He became minister of Perth, one of the six men named John who wrote the First Book of Discipline, and a framer of the Scots Confession. A canon lawyer's training made him unusually useful in the ordering of the new church courts, and his knowledge of the Roman system from inside made him a formidable opponent of it. His son wrote the history of the Kirk that preserves much of what we know of the period. A man who comes over carrying the other side's expertise is a particular kind of gift, and the church that receives him must be careful to receive the man and not merely the expertise. “searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines nuncio as an ambassador from the pope to some prince or state, and canon law as the body of ecclesiastical law.
webster_full: NUN'CIO, n. An ambassador from the pope to some prince or state; a papal envoy.
CAN'ON LAW, n. The body of ecclesiastical law adopted in the Christian church.
CONVERT', v. To change from one religion to another; to turn from one persuasion to the contrary.
DIS'CIPLINE, n. In a church, the execution of the laws by which it is governed; the system of rules and order.

corruption_summary: The papal nuncio to Scotland who examined the case he was sent to suppress and changed sides.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the treatment of such a conversion as a biography of temperament — a restless man who was going to change sooner or later — which spares the reader from having to ask what he found. Row was a trained canon lawyer sent on a commission, and what turned him was the examination of the documents and the Scriptures he had been dispatched to answer.

The principle to recover is that the Bereans are commended for exactly this and that Scripture treats verification as noble rather than disloyal. “These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11). Paul describes the cost in his own case with an accountant's vocabulary: “But what things were gain to me, those I counted loss for Christ” (Php 3:7). A doctorate in canon law and a nuncio's commission are entries on that ledger.

pos: n. (John Erskine of Dun, 1509–1591, laird, superintendent of Angus and Mearns)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Scots Erskine, from a Renfrewshire place-name; Dun, a hill fort.
biblical_def: John Erskine of Dun was a Mearns laird who brought the first teacher of Greek into Scotland at his own expense, founded a school at Montrose from which a generation of reformers came, and spent fifty years as the most trusted layman in the Scottish church. He was provost of Montrose, a privy councillor, four times moderator of the General Assembly though never ordained in the usual way, and superintendent of Angus and Mearns from 1560. His particular gift was that both sides would listen to him: he carried messages between the Lords of the Congregation and the regent, between the Kirk and Queen Mary, and between Knox and men Knox had offended. He was courteous where Knox was blunt and immovable where it counted. A reformation needs both kinds and usually only celebrates one. The school at Montrose is the quieter monument: George Wishart taught Greek in it, and what was learned there went out through the whole east of Scotland. “Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God” (Mat 5:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines laird as a lord, the proprietor of a landed estate in Scotland, and moderator as the president of an ecclesiastical assembly.
webster_full: LAIRD, n. In the Scots dialect, a lord; the proprietor of a landed estate.
MOD'ERATOR, n. The president of a meeting or assembly, particularly of an ecclesiastical body.
PROV'OST, n. The chief magistrate of a city or borough in Scotland.
MED'IATE, v. To interpose between parties at variance for the purpose of reconciling them.

corruption_summary: The Mearns laird who paid for Scotland's first Greek teacher and carried messages everyone would read.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern suspicion of the mediator, who is read as a man without convictions precisely because both parties will speak to him. Erskine had convictions and the record shows where he would not move: he subscribed the Confession, governed his province as superintendent, and sat in the Assembly against the court when it mattered. What he refused was unnecessary offence, which is a different thing from compromise.

The principle to recover is that peacemaking is a beatitude and not a temperament, and that Scripture attaches a startling title to it: “Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God” (Mat 5:9). Paul bounds the duty honestly on both sides — “If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men” (Rom 12:18) — which concedes that it is not always possible and still lays the whole of one's own part on the believer.

pos: n. (John Spottiswoode, 1510–1585, superintendent of Lothian and co-author of the First Book of Discipline)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Scots Spottiswoode, from a Berwickshire place-name.
biblical_def: John Spottiswoode studied at Glasgow, went to England, and was there instructed by Cranmer, who ordained him; he came back to Scotland and was one of the six Johns who drew up the First Book of Discipline in 1560. He served as superintendent of Lothian, the largest and most difficult of the five provinces, for twenty-five years, and he was moderator of the General Assembly. His particular contribution is the Book of Discipline itself, which is one of the boldest documents of the Reformation: a plan for a national church in which every parish has a preaching minister, every town a school, every notable town a college, and the poor are maintained out of the old church patrimony. The nobility, who had taken that patrimony, refused to fund it, and the plan was never carried out as written. His son became archbishop of St Andrews and the king's instrument against the presbyterian party, which the father did not live to see. “Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it” (Pro 22:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines patrimony as a right or estate inherited from one's ancestors, and discipline as the system of rules by which a church is governed.
webster_full: PAT'RIMONY, n. A right or estate inherited from one's ancestors; a church estate or revenue.
DIS'CIPLINE, n. In a church, the execution of the laws by which it is governed; the system of rules and order.
PRO'VINCE, n. A district over which a governor or superintendent has jurisdiction.
ENDOW'MENT, n. The act of settling a fund or permanent provision for the support of a church or institution.

corruption_summary: Lothian's superintendent, and the Book of Discipline the nobles would not pay for.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the presentation of the First Book of Discipline as a utopian document that failed for being impractical. It failed for a stated and recorded reason: the lords of Scotland had taken the revenues of the old church into their own hands and declined to release them. The plan was costed against a patrimony that existed. It was defeated by appetite, not by arithmetic.

The principle to recover is that Scripture attaches real material obligations to the church's ministry and its poor, and that these are not optional adornments of a budget. “Let the elders that rule well be counted worthy of double honour, especially they who labour in the word and doctrine” (1Ti 5:17) is a wage. The schooling of the young is laid on the same conscience: “Train up a child in the way he should go” (Pro 22:6). A reformation that reorders the doctrine and leaves the money where it fell has done half the work.

pos: n. (James Melville, 1556–1614, Scottish minister and diarist)
etymology: Hebrew Yaaqob, a supplanter, through Latin Jacobus; Scots Melville, from a Norman place-name, the bad town.
biblical_def: James Melville was the nephew of Andrew Melville, a professor at St Andrews, a minister at Kilrenny in Fife, and the author of the best personal record anyone left of the Scottish church in its second generation. His diary is unlike almost anything else of the century: a man writing down what he actually remembered of being a frightened small boy at school, of hearing Knox preach at St Andrews in his last year and being so moved he could not hold his pen, of the terror of his uncle's confrontations with the king, of the fishing village he served and the people in it. He stood with Andrew Melville for the presbyterian cause against James VI's bishops, was summoned to London with him in 1606, and was confined for the rest of his life to Newcastle, never allowed home to Kilrenny. He died in exile from a parish forty miles away. The diary is the kind of document that keeps a church honest about its own past, because it records what the official histories tidy. “to write unto thee in order” (Luk 1:3).

corruption_summary: The Fife minister whose diary records what the official histories tidy away.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the kind of church history that remembers only the resolutions. Melville's diary preserves the texture that gets lost: a schoolboy's fear, the sound of an old man in a pulpit, the parish he was kept from for eight years. Without such records a church's memory of itself becomes a list of assemblies and a roll of principles, and it loses the ability to recognise its own condition in another generation.

The principle to recover is that the handing on of what God has done is specific and narrative, and Scripture models it that way. “We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD, and his strength, and his wonderful works that he hath done” (Psa 78:4). Works that he hath done — particular things, in particular places. Luke claims the same method for his own writing: “to write unto thee in order” (Luk 1:3).

pos: n. (Robert Pont, 1524–1606, Scottish minister, moderator and senator of the College of Justice)
etymology: Germanic Robert, bright in fame; French Pont, a bridge, from Latin pons.
biblical_def: Robert Pont was six times moderator of the General Assembly, minister of St Cuthbert's in Edinburgh, provost of Trinity College, and for some years a Lord of Session — a judge of Scotland's supreme civil court while serving as a minister, which the Assembly eventually decided a minister should not do and he gave up. He helped revise the Second Book of Discipline, worked on the Scottish psalm book, and wrote on chronology and on the reckoning of the year. His career raises the question of the two kingdoms in an unusually concrete form, because he held offices in both at once and the church itself made him choose. The Scottish answer was not that the civil office is unclean, nor that the minister is above it, but that the two callings are distinct and one man cannot discharge both: the church has no sword and the state has no pulpit, and a man sitting in the Court of Session cannot also sit in judgment on that court from a pulpit. “Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's” (Mat 22:21).

webster_full: SES'SION, n. The actual sitting of a court, council or legislative body; the time of such sitting.
JURISDIC'TION, n. The legal power or authority of doing justice in cases of complaint; the power of executing the laws.
MOD'ERATOR, n. The president of an ecclesiastical assembly.
CHRONOL'OGY, n. The science of time; the method of measuring or computing time by regular divisions.

corruption_summary: Six times moderator, and a minister made to choose between the pulpit and the bench.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse runs in both directions from this case. One side reads the Assembly's ruling as clericalism, the church fencing its men off from public life; the other reads it as a doctrine that civil office is beneath a Christian. Neither is the Scottish position. The civil magistracy is honourable and is itself called a ministry of God; what the Assembly denied was that one man may hold both offices at once.

The principle to recover is the distinction the Lord draws without abolishing either side of it: “Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's” (Mat 22:21). Both have things that are theirs. Paul gives the practical reason a minister should not be entangled: “No man that warreth entangleth himself with the affairs of this life; that he may please him who hath chosen him to be a soldier” (2Ti 2:4).

pos: n. (David Ferguson, d. 1598, minister of Dunfermline and collector of Scots proverbs)
etymology: Hebrew David, beloved; Gaelic Fearghus, man of vigour, with the patronymic son.
biblical_def: David Ferguson was a Dundee glover with no university training who became minister of Dunfermline, twice moderator of the General Assembly, and one of the plainest preachers in Scotland. He is remembered for two things. The first is a sermon preached before the regent and the nobility in 1572, printed afterwards, in which he told the men holding the old church revenues to their faces that they were robbing the ministry and the poor, and named it theft. The second is a collection of Scots proverbs, the earliest of its kind, gathered because he used them constantly in the pulpit and thought the common speech of his people was the right vessel for the truth. The two things belong together. A man who preaches in the proverbs of the market can say something to a nobleman that a Latinist cannot, and be understood by everyone in the building while he says it. The substance of what he said to them was older than Dunfermline: “Will a man rob God? Yet ye have robbed me” (Mal 3:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines proverb as a short sentence often repeated, expressing a well known truth, and sacrilege as the crime of violating or profaning sacred things.
webster_full: PROV'ERB, n. A short sentence often repeated, expressing a well known truth or common fact ascertained by experience.
SAC'RILEGE, n. The crime of violating or profaning sacred things; the alienating to common purposes what has been appropriated to religious uses.
GLOV'ER, n. One whose occupation is to make and sell gloves.
PUL'PIT, n. An elevated place or inclosed stage in a church, in which the preacher stands.

Will a man rob God? Yet ye have robbed me. But ye say, Wherein have we robbed thee? In tithes and offerings.

Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be meat in mine house, and prove me now herewith, saith the LORD of hosts, if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there shall not be room enough to receive it.
Let the elders that rule well be counted worthy of double honour, especially they who labour in the word and doctrine.
So likewise ye, except ye utter by the tongue words easy to be understood, how shall it be known what is spoken? for ye shall speak into the air.
corruption_summary: The glover who preached sacrilege to the regent's face and collected the proverbs of his people.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the assumption that plain speech is a limitation accepted by men who could not manage anything better. Ferguson had no university and did not pretend to one, and he chose the proverbs deliberately as the instrument that would carry furthest in the building he was preaching in. The sermon of 1572 is the proof: a lecture on sacrilege delivered in the common tongue to the men committing it, with no place for anyone present to hide behind not having followed.

The principle to recover is that Scripture names the withholding of the church's maintenance as robbery of God and does so in the bluntest available words. “Will a man rob God? Yet ye have robbed me. But ye say, Wherein have we robbed thee? In tithes and offerings” (Mal 3:8). The remedy is equally concrete: “Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be meat in mine house” (Mal 3:10). Paul applies the same obligation to the ministry of the word (1Ti 5:17).

pos: n. (Alexander Arbuthnot, 1538–1583, principal of King's College Aberdeen)
etymology: Greek Alexandros, defender of men; Scots Arbuthnot, from a Kincardineshire place-name.
biblical_def: Alexander Arbuthnot was principal of King's College in Aberdeen from 1569, twice moderator of the General Assembly, a civil lawyer trained at Bourges, and a man the king disliked because he would not keep the north quiet. Aberdeen was the most conservative corner of Scotland and the college was full of men who had not wanted the Reformation; Arbuthnot reformed it from inside over fourteen years, teaching theology himself and refusing to be driven out. He helped frame the Second Book of Discipline. He also lent his name and his money to the printing of the first Bible produced in Scotland, the Bassandyne Bible of 1579, printed at Edinburgh with Thomas Bassandyne, which an act of parliament then required every substantial household in the realm to buy. He died at forty-five, worn out, having written to a friend that the care of the college and the quarrels of the Kirk had consumed him. “And they taught in Judah, and had the book of the law of the LORD with them, and went about throughout all the cities of Judah, and taught the people” (2Ch 17:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines principal as the chief or head of a college, and impression as the edition of a book printed at one time.
webster_full: PRIN'CIPAL, n. A chief or head; the president, governor or chief in authority, as of a college.
IMPRES'SION, n. The copies of a book printed at one time; an edition.
COL'LEGE, n. A society of persons engaged in the pursuits of literature, including the officers and students.
HOUSE'HOLD, n. Those who dwell under the same roof and compose a family.
scriptures: And they taught in Judah, and had the book of the law of the LORD with them, and went about throughout all the cities of Judah, and taught the people.
Deu 6:6
And these words, which I command thee this day, shall be in thine heart:

Psa 19:8
The statutes of the LORD are right, rejoicing the heart: the commandment of the LORD is pure, enlightening the eyes.
corruption_summary: Aberdeen's principal, and the first Bible printed in Scotland.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern instinct that a law requiring households to own a Bible must be mere coercion, a state imposing religion by statute. The 1579 act is better read alongside what it presupposed: a country in which the book had been unavailable in the common tongue within living memory, and a church that wanted it in every substantial house before the generation that remembered the change had died.

The principle to recover is that the word is to be carried to the people where they live rather than kept where the learned are. Jehoshaphat's teaching commission is the model and the detail is the point: “And they taught in Judah, and had the book of the law of the LORD with them, and went about throughout all the cities of Judah, and taught the people” (2Ch 17:9). They went about, and they took the book. The household end of the same duty is Moses's: “these words, which I command thee this day, shall be in thine heart” (Deu 6:6).

pos: n. (Paul Methven, fl. 1558–1566, early preacher at Dundee, deposed for adultery)
etymology: Latin Paulus, little, small; Scots Methven, from a Perthshire place-name.
biblical_def: Paul Methven was a baker of Dundee who began preaching in 1558, before the Reformation was secure, and gathered what was in effect the first reformed congregation in Scotland. He was summoned for it, outlawed, and was one of the preachers whose prosecution brought matters to the crisis of 1559. When the settlement came he was minister of Jedburgh. In 1563 he was convicted of adultery with a servant in his own house, fled to England, and was deposed. He came back three years later and sought restoration; the General Assembly required him to stand in sackcloth at the kirk door of Jedburgh and of Edinburgh and of Dundee on successive days, barefoot and bareheaded, and he began the penance and could not finish it. He went back to England and died there in obscurity. The Kirk neither pretended the sin away nor denied that restoration was possible; it required the discipline to be as public as the scandal, which is the hard and right answer. “Them that sin rebuke before all, that others also may fear” (1Ti 5:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines penance as an ecclesiastical punishment inflicted for a sinful act, and depose as to degrade, to divest of office.
webster_full: PEN'ANCE, n. The suffering, labour or pain to which a person voluntarily subjects himself, or which is imposed as satisfaction for sin.
DEPO'SE, v. To degrade; to remove from a throne or other high station; to divest of office.
DIS'CIPLINE, n. In a church, the execution of the laws by which it is governed; correction; chastisement.
RESTORA'TION, n. The act of replacing in a former state; renewal; re-establishment.
scriptures: Them that sin rebuke before all, that others also may fear.
A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach;
Gal 6:1
Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted.
Wherefore let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall.
corruption_summary: The first reformed congregation in Scotland, and a minister the Kirk deposed and could not restore.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern management of ministerial scandal, which tends to one of two errors. Either the fall is treated as disqualifying forever and the man is discarded, or it is handled quietly, the discipline is private, the congregation is told as little as possible, and the man reappears elsewhere. The Scottish Assembly did neither. It held restoration open and it set the price in public, because the injury had been public.

The principle to recover is that Paul attaches a purpose to the publicity of the rebuke and it is not the humiliation of the offender. “Them that sin rebuke before all, that others also may fear” (1Ti 5:20). The watching church is the reason. And the spirit required of those administering it is named as carefully as the act: “restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted” (Gal 6:1).
